plain_title: When orgasm is rare, delayed, or muted, and it bothers you
one_liner: Orgasms that are absent, much delayed, rare, or much less intense than wanted, causing distress, for six months or more.
in_simple_words: Female orgasmic disorder is when a woman regularly can't reach orgasm, takes much longer than she'd like, or finds orgasms much less intense, despite adequate arousal and stimulation, for at least six months, and it troubles her. Some women have never had an orgasm; for others it changes after illness, childbirth, or medication. Not orgasming from penetration alone is normal, not a disorder. The most effective treatments teach women about their own bodies and responses, and are highly successful.
what_it_can_feel_like: I was 34 and thought there was something wrong with me. It turned out nobody had ever told me how most women's bodies actually work.
After my antidepressant, orgasms just vanished. Talking to my doctor was awkward for about thirty seconds and then it was fine.
common_signs: Orgasm absent, rare, or much delayed despite enough stimulation
Orgasms much less intense than before or than wanted
Lasting at least six months, most of the time

myths_vs_facts.myth: Women should orgasm from penetration alone; if not, something's wrong.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Most women need direct clitoral stimulation to orgasm. Not orgasming from penetration alone is the norm, not a disorder.

myths_vs_facts.myth: If it hasn't happened by now, it never will.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Structured programmes that teach women about their own responses have very high success rates, including for women who've never had an orgasm.

how_common.plain: Around 1 in 20 US women report orgasm difficulties that distress them, and about 1 in 5 report difficulty overall. Figures vary a lot by how questions are asked.

what_helps.plain_summary: Psychosexual therapy is the main treatment. Structured self-exploration programmes, taught by a therapist, have the strongest evidence, particularly for women who've never had an orgasm. Sensate focus exercises with a partner, CBT for anxiety and self-consciousness, and education about anatomy all help. A doctor reviews medications (some antidepressants are a common cause), hormones, and medical conditions. No medication has good evidence for improving orgasm in women.
evidence_based_options: Psychosexual therapy including structured self-exploration programmes
CBT for anxiety, self-consciousness, or negative beliefs about sex
Medication and medical review by a doctor
self_help_that_supports_care: Learning about your own anatomy and responses from reputable sources
Reducing goal-focus; pleasure without a deadline
Talking with a partner about what works
Asking a doctor about medication effects rather than stopping them

when_to_reach_out: If orgasm difficulties are bothering you, talk to a psychosexual therapist or a doctor, especially if things changed after a medication, illness, or childbirth. The treatments are gentle and effective.
is_not: Sexual difficulties that are occasional, explained by a medical condition or medication, caused by severe relationship distress, or that don't bother you aren't diagnosed as a disorder. Not reaching orgasm from penetration alone, or needing more time than a partner, is common and not a disorder.
hope_note: Most women who seek help for orgasm difficulties get what they came for. Education alone changes a great deal.

content_notes: Sex-positive, shame-free wording; no explicit technique descriptions. Medication named only in general terms.
